info.desc: "The Joshua Tree" is the fifth studio album by Irish rock band U2, released March 9, 1987 on Island Records. Recording sessions took place from July to November of 1986 at Windmill Lane Studios in Dublin. The album features the band's exploration of roots rock, with their music exhibiting influences from blues-rock, folk rock, Southern rock, and gospel music. Lyrically, "The Joshua Tree" depicts the band's fascination with America and many of the ideas it stands for. The album was produced and engineered by Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois. The album increased the band's stature "from heroes to superstars," according .

podcast.body: A key theme for "The Joshua Tree," hinted at by the original title "Two Americas," arose from the band's extensive touring in the United States in the years prior to the album. During this period, U2 connected with American artists like Bob Dylan and deepened their relationship with European artists such as The Rolling Stones, who were deeply enamored with American culture and music. This exposure led Bono to feel U2 lacked musical roots, prompting the band to study and integrate classic American music, including Country, Blues, and classic American Rock, drawing inspiration from early electric guitars influenced by Chuck Berry. Beyond music, Bono immersed himself in classic American literature and observed the social and cultural aspects, particularly the "breakdown of the American Dream," which became a significant source of inspiration for the album's themes. "tenemos muchas influencias del Country, tenemos muchas influencias del blues, tenemos muchas influencias del rock clásico americano, incluso de las primeras guitarras eléctricas en Chuck Berry."

podcast.body: For "The Joshua Tree" and subsequent albums, U2 significantly refined their composition methods. Previously, the band would enter recording sessions with songs still creatively "raw" and sometimes with unfinished lyrics, completing the composition process during recording. With "The Joshua Tree," Bono began to treat lyric writing almost like poetry, working on them in isolation with a highly literary approach. The rest of the band would then compose the music based on these nearly completed lyrics. This more complex and professional method differed greatly from the approach U2 used in their earlier albums. "Bono empieza a trabajar las letras casi como poemas, a escribir las ensolitario, a trabajar las de manera completamente literaria, mientras que la banda después con unas letras casi terminadas empieza a trabajar en la composición de la música."

podcast.body: Released on March 9, 1987, this album is U2's fifth and has sold over 25 million copies, establishing it as one of the best-selling albums of all time. It reached number one in two dozen countries, and five of its eleven songs were released as singles, with several selling over a million copies. The supporting tour expanded from arenas to stadiums, leading to the live record "Live from Paris" and the documentary film "Rattle and Hum." The album earned U2 two Grammys: Album of the Year and Group of the Year, solidifying their status as one of the biggest bands globally. In 2014, it was added to the US Library of Congress for its cultural, historical, and aesthetic significance. "The Joshua Tree set up the band as one of the biggest in the world, and over the coming decade, they would become the biggest band in the world."

podcast.body: The album marked a turning point for U2, with its political content becoming increasingly explicit. The band was deeply affected by various late 1980s events, including the Civil War in El Salvador, the plight of mothers in South America who had lost children in civil wars and dictatorships, mining strikes in the United Kingdom, and the persistent religious terrorism in Northern Ireland. These events provided a rich tapestry for the album's direct political commentary, which became a defining feature of "The Joshua Tree" and subsequent U2 albums. "tenemos la Guerra Civil del Salvador, tenemos las famosas comadronas en su América, que habían perdido a sus hijos en las trasitadulas y las guerras civiles, tenemos las vulgas de la minería en el Reconido, tenemos las continuas duchas todavía el terrorismo religioso que había en Irlanda del Norte, y eso viene a ser un poco la guinda del pastel."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.body: The album was not originally intended to be called "The Joshua Tree". Its initial proposed titles were "The Desert Songs" and later "Two Americas". The final name change occurred when the band went to the Mojave Desert in California, specifically Joshua Tree National Park, for the album's cover photography. The iconic Joshua Tree photographed for the cover still stands there today, marked with a commemorative plaque. The discarded original titles, "The Desert Songs" and "Two Americas," better hint at the album's thematic content. "Finalmente se terminó cambiando del Yosu Atri cuando la banda fue a hacerse las fotografías para la portada y para todo el árbol del disco, eso fueron al desierto de Mojave, en California, al Parque Nacional de Yosu."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.body: The album was produced by the highly influential Brian Eno and his personal friend Daniel Lanois. Brian Eno had previously produced several U2 albums and continued to work with them afterwards, with Bono attributing much of U2's success to Eno's significant production work. Both producers took an unconventional approach, not only handling classic production duties but also playing instruments and contributing backing vocals on some songs during the recording of "The Joshua Tree." "tanto, Brian Nino como Daniel Lanois, a trabajar durante el álbum no solo en trabajos de producción, sino que tocaron instrumentos durante la grabación del álbum, pero incluso a sus voces figuran en los coros algunas de las canciones."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.body: The album's working title "The Desert Songs" alludes to its spiritual journey theme, which sparked ongoing debate about its Christian or religious connotations. During this period, Bono embarked on a significant spiritual process, blending humanitarian efforts (such as his trips to Africa to raise money) with mystical and religious experiences. This led to themes of inner exploration, self-discovery, and human morality throughout the album, with numerous references to God, faith, and spiritual seeking. These elements, combined with the "Joshua Tree" imagery, contribute to the album's ambiguous but evident spiritual and potentially Christian undertones. "Bono comenzó un enorme fase de proceso espiritual durante esta época, de hecho, cuando le empezó a hacer sus viajes a África, a conocer las abrones de África, lluchar por este tipo de causas, a recalar dinero."

podcast.body: This album marks its 30th anniversary this week since its publication in 1987. It was the third consecutive album for U2 to receive maximum critical acclaim and remains the band's best-selling album to date, with approximately 28 million copies sold. It holds the 26th position on Rolling Stone magazine's list of the greatest albums in history. In 1987, it earned U2 their first Grammy for Best Album of the Year and quickly rose to number one on sales charts. Curiously, it also positioned at number 36 on the list of best Christian albums in 1987. The album was recorded rapidly, taking only three months despite its high quality. During its creation, U2 began refining their composition methods, moving towards a more structured approach where Bono would work on lyrics as poems, and the band would then compose the music with almost finished texts. The band's positive mood following the success of their previous three albums also contributed to this process. "Al día de hoy, ha vendido unos 28 millones de copias y sigue siendo el álbum más vendido de la banda U2."
